verse.text: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, to the assembly of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: grace to you and peace.
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

Silvanus is generally identified with the Silas of Acts, who with Paul and Timothy first brought the message to Thessalonica, the chief city of the Roman province of Macedonia. The three are named as joint senders, which is why the letter speaks as “we.”

note.traditional: Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” matching Paul’s usual greeting in other letters. The shorter form is found in important early witnesses and is generally judged original; the longer is most likely a scribal assimilation.

verse.text: We always give thanks to God for all of you, mentioning you in our prayers, constantly
remembering before our God and Father your work of faith, your labor of love, and your endurance of hope in our Lord Jesus Christ.

note.term: your work of faith, your labor of love, and your endurance of hope
note.traditional: your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope

verse.note: The three Greek genitives are left as plain “of” phrases. Most interpreters take them as naming the source: work that springs from faith, labor prompted by love, endurance sustained by hope. The hope is “of our Lord Jesus Christ,” understood here as hope directed toward him.

note.traditional: in the sight of God and our Father

verse.note: In the Greek this phrase comes at the end of the verse. It is taken here with “remembering,” that is, remembering in prayer before God. It could instead describe the Thessalonians’ faith, love, and hope as lived out in God’s presence.

verse.text: We know, brothers and sisters loved by God, that he has chosen you,
verse.note: The Greek plural was regularly used for a mixed group of siblings, and here it addresses the whole community, women as well as men. “Brothers” alone would now suggest that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

The Greek is a noun phrase, literally “your choosing” or “your election.” “Election” is the traditional rendering and remains a standard theological term, but in ordinary English it now suggests voting. The word means God’s act of choosing, which the verbal phrase conveys directly.

verse.text: because our good news did not come to you in word only, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction—just as you know what kind of people we proved to be among you for your sake.
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it now sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. Many modern translations already alternate between the two.

The word can mean complete certainty or, less likely here, fullness. It is not stated whose conviction is meant. The following clause about the missionaries’ conduct suggests the assurance with which they preached, though some take it of the certainty produced in the hearers.

verse.text: And you became imitators of us and of the Lord, for you received the word in much affliction with joy from the Holy Spirit,
so that you became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and in Achaia.
verse.note: These were the two Roman provinces that together covered Greece: Macedonia in the north, with Thessalonica as its chief city, and Achaia in the south, which included Corinth and Athens. Thessalonica lay on a major road and had a busy port, which helps explain how news from there traveled quickly.

verse.text: For from you the word of the Lord has rung out, not only in Macedonia and Achaia—in every place your faith in God has gone out, so that we have no need to say anything.
For they themselves report about us what kind of reception we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve a living and true God
verse.note: The Greek has no article here, and most translations supply “the.” The rendering “a living and true God” keeps the stress on the contrast with idols, which in Jewish polemic were lifeless and false. It does not imply that there are other such gods.

verse.text: and to wait for his Son from the heavens, whom he raised from the dead—Jesus, who rescues us from the coming wrath.
verse.note: The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase carried over from the Hebrew Scriptures. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept wherever the Greek has it and God’s dwelling is meant.

The Greek is a present participle, which can describe Jesus timelessly as “our rescuer.” Older versions rendered it as past (“delivered”), while many modern ones use the present. Since the wrath is described as “coming,” the rescue in view is chiefly a future one.

verse.text: For you yourselves know, brothers and sisters, that our visit to you was not in vain,
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community. “Brothers” alone now suggests to many readers that only men are addressed. Several modern translations make the same choice; others keep “brothers” and explain it in a footnote.

The Greek word means “empty.” It may mean the visit was not fruitless, or that it was not hollow—lacking in substance, sincerity, or power. The following verses, which defend the character of the mission, give some support to the second reading; the rendering here follows the more common first one.

verse.text: but though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi, as you know, we found boldness in our God to speak to you the good news of God amid a great struggle.
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used among other things for imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has since become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

verse.text: For our appeal does not come from error or from impure motives, nor is it made with deceit,
but just as we have been tested and found fit by God to be entrusted with the good news, so we speak, not to please people but to please God, who tests our hearts.
For we never came with flattering words, as you know, nor with a cover for greed, God is our witness,
nor were we seeking glory from people, whether from you or from others,
though as apostles of Christ we could have made our weight felt. Instead we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishing her own children.
verse.note: Literally “been in weight.” The phrase can mean being a financial burden (compare verse 9, where a related verb means “to burden”) or carrying weight in the sense of insisting on one’s importance and authority. The context, which speaks of seeking glory in verse 6 and of gentleness in what follows, slightly favors the second, but both may be in view.

Manuscripts are divided between “gentle” (ēpioi) and “infants” (nēpioi), which differ by a single letter that could easily be doubled or dropped after the preceding word. The earliest manuscripts mostly read “infants,” and some critical editions print it; the edition translated here reads “gentle,” as do most English versions, because it fits the image that follows. The question remains disputed.

The Greek word usually denotes a nurse, often a wet nurse hired to care for another family’s children. Paul specifies “her own children,” so the picture is either of a mother nursing or of a professional nurse giving her own children the tenderest care of all.

verse.text: So, yearning for you, we were glad to share with you not only the good news of God but also our own lives, because you had become so dear to us.
For you remember, brothers and sisters, our labor and toil: working night and day so as not to burden any of you, we proclaimed to you the good news of God.
You are witnesses, and so is God, of how devoutly and justly and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believe,
just as you know how we dealt with each one of you like a father with his own children,
appealing to you and encouraging you and solemnly charging you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.

And for this reason we too thank God unceasingly: when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of people but as what it truly is, the word of God, which is also at work in you who believe.

For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of the assemblies of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea, because you too suffered the same things from your own compatriots as they did from the Jews
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people—a city’s citizen assembly, or in the Greek Old Testament Israel gathered before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses “assembly” throughout. “Church” is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to.

The Greek can be read as limiting (“those Jews who killed…”) or as a description of the whole people (“the Jews, who killed…”); the translation leaves out the comma, taking it as the former. Paul, himself a Jew, is comparing persecution in Thessalonica with what the assemblies in Judea suffered from their own people, and some would translate “Judeans” here. A minority of scholars regard verses 14–16 as a later insertion, though no manuscript lacks them.

verse.text: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets and drove us out, who do not please God and are opposed to all people,
preventing us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But the wrath has come upon them at last.
verse.note: The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations.” In the plural, in Jewish usage, it refers to the non-Jewish peoples, and it is translated “Gentiles” in that sense and “nations” elsewhere. It is one word in Greek.

The Greek phrase can mean “at last,” “completely,” “to the end,” or “forever,” and translations differ. It is also unclear what Paul has in mind by wrath having come: a recent calamity, or a future judgment spoken of as certain. Scholars have proposed several events from the late 40s, but none can be confirmed.

verse.text: But we, brothers and sisters, orphaned from you for a short time—in person, not in heart—made all the greater effort, with great desire, to see your face.

note.traditional: taken from you; torn away from you

verse.note: The Greek verb means to be made an orphan, and it could be used more loosely of any painful bereavement, including parents separated from children. It continues the family imagery of the chapter, where Paul has compared himself to a nursing mother and a father.

verse.text: For we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, more than once—but Satan blocked our way.
For what is our hope or joy or the crown we will boast of before our Lord Jesus at his coming—is it not indeed you?
verse.note: The Greek word means “arrival” or “presence,” and it was a standard term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, an occasion marked by public welcome and honors. Paul uses it for the expected arrival of Jesus as Lord. The “crown” in the same verse is the wreath awarded to a victor or an honored person.

verse.text: Yes, you are our glory and our joy.
So when we could bear it no longer, we thought it best to be left behind in Athens alone,

note.term: we thought it best to be left behind in Athens alone

verse.note: The letter is sent by Paul, Silvanus and Timothy, and it is unclear whether “we” here means Paul and Silvanus together or is Paul’s way of speaking of himself. Verse 5 repeats the same statement in the singular (“I sent”), which leads many interpreters to think Paul mainly means himself. The translation keeps the Greek’s plural and singular as they stand.

verse.text: and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s coworker in the good news of Christ, to strengthen and encourage you for the sake of your faith,
verse.note: Manuscripts differ here: some read “God’s servant” (or “minister”), some “God’s coworker,” and some combine the two. Most scholars think “God’s coworker” is original and that scribes softened so bold a description. The phrase could also be taken as “our coworker for God,” but the plainer sense is that Timothy works alongside God.

The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today is heard as a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: so that no one would be shaken by these afflictions. For you yourselves know that this is what we are appointed for.
verse.note: This verb occurs only here in the New Testament. Its earlier use was of a dog wagging its tail, and from that of fawning or flattering, so some interpreters take the sense to be “beguiled” or “talked out of their faith” by smooth words. Most translators and lexicons take the meaning here to be “disturbed” or “unsettled,” which is followed in the text.

The word is often rendered “tribulation,” which many readers now hear as the name of a specific end-time period. In the period it was an ordinary word for hardship or oppression pressing on someone, here the hostility the Thessalonians met from their neighbors. “Affliction” is itself a long-established rendering, and the related verb in verse 4 is translated “suffer affliction” to keep the link visible.

verse.text: Indeed, when we were with you, we kept telling you in advance that we were going to suffer affliction—and so it happened, as you know.
That is why, when I could bear it no longer, I sent to find out about your faith, for fear that the tempter had somehow tempted you and our labor would turn out to be for nothing.
But now Timothy has come to us from you and has brought us the good news of your faith and love. He has told us that you always remember us kindly and long to see us, just as we long to see you.
verse.note: Paul uses the same verb he normally reserves for announcing the message about Christ. This is the only place in his letters where it refers to other good news, and the choice of word shows how much Timothy’s report meant to him.

verse.text: For this reason, brothers and sisters, in all our distress and affliction we were encouraged about you through your faith,
verse.note: The Greek plural, traditionally “brothers” or “brethren,” was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as members of one family. Since Paul is addressing the whole congregation, “brothers and sisters” conveys what the first hearers understood. Several modern translations do the same; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

verse.text: for now we live, if you are standing firm in the Lord.
For what thanks can we give back to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice because of you before our God,
as night and day we pray with the utmost earnestness to see you face to face and to supply what is lacking in your faith?
Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you.
verse.note: The prayer has two subjects, “our God and Father” and “our Lord Jesus,” but the Greek verb is singular. Greek can use a singular verb with a compound subject, so the grammar alone proves little, but many interpreters note how closely Paul joins God and Jesus as the one to whom prayer is addressed. The word “himself” could grammatically cover both subjects or the Father alone.

verse.text: And may the Lord make you increase and overflow in love for one another and for everyone, just as we do for you,
so as to strengthen your hearts to be blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his holy ones.
verse.note: The Greek word means arrival and the presence that follows. It was commonly used for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, an occasion that involved public preparation and welcome. Paul uses it in this letter for the expected arrival of Jesus as Lord.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul normally uses the word for all believers, but here many scholars think it refers to angels accompanying the Lord, echoing Zechariah 14:5 (“the Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with him”). Others take it as believers who have died, or as both together; “holy ones” leaves the question open, as the Greek does. Some manuscripts add “Amen” at the end of the verse.

verse.text: Finally then, brothers and sisters, we ask and urge you in the Lord Jesus: just as you received from us how you ought to walk and please God—as indeed you are walking—do so more and more.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole congregation. “Brothers” alone now suggests men only, so the fuller phrase is used; several modern translations do the same. The singular in verse 6 is rendered “a brother or sister” on the same principle.

verse.text: For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
For this is the will of God, your holiness: that you keep away from sexual immorality;
verse.note: The Greek noun, used three times in verses 3–7, means the state or process of being set apart for God. “Sanctification” is the traditional rendering but has become a technical theological term; “holiness” is plainer and lets the reader hear the link with the “Holy” Spirit in verse 8, which is the same word family.

verse.text: that each of you know how to gain control of your own body in holiness and honor,

note.term: gain control of your own body

verse.note: Literally “to acquire (or possess) his own vessel.” “Vessel” is a metaphor that can mean one’s own body (possibly with a specifically sexual reference) or one’s wife, giving “to take a wife for himself.” The verb more often means “acquire,” which favors the second reading, but most recent translations take it of mastering one’s body. Scholars remain divided.

verse.text: not in lustful passion like the Gentiles who do not know God;
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural it is the standard Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples, and is rendered “nations” or “Gentiles” in this translation according to sense. Most of the Thessalonian believers were themselves non-Jews by birth, so Paul is using the word for those outside the community who do not know Israel’s God.

verse.text: that no one overstep and take advantage of a brother or sister in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, just as we told you before and solemnly warned you.

note.traditional: in any matter / in this matter

verse.note: The Greek is literally “in the matter.” Most interpreters take it as the sexual conduct just discussed, so that the wrong is done to another person through sexual misconduct. The word can also mean a business dealing, and some read the verse as a new topic, fraud in commerce.

verse.text: For God did not call us for impurity but in holiness.
Therefore whoever rejects this is rejecting not a human being but God, who also gives his Holy Spirit to you.
Now about love for the brothers and sisters, you have no need for anyone to write to you, for you yourselves are taught by God to love one another;
and indeed you do this toward all the brothers and sisters throughout Macedonia. But we urge you, brothers and sisters, to do so more and more,
and to make it your ambition to live quietly, to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands, just as we instructed you,
so that you may walk properly toward outsiders and have need of no one.

note.traditional: have lack of nothing / be dependent on no one

verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine (“no one”) or neuter (“nothing”). The first gives the sense of not depending on others for support; the second, of lacking nothing. Either fits the instruction to work with one’s own hands.

verse.text: But we do not want you to be uninformed, brothers and sisters, about those who are asleep, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who have no hope.
verse.note: Sleep was a common euphemism for death in both Greek and Jewish usage, and the readers would have understood at once that Paul means members of the community who have died. The image is kept because Paul uses it deliberately alongside the language of rising.

verse.text: For if we believe that Jesus died and rose, so also, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.

note.traditional: them also which sleep in Jesus

verse.note: The phrase “through Jesus” can attach to “will bring” (God will bring them through Jesus), as here, or to “fallen asleep” (those who have fallen asleep through Jesus, that is, who died as his people). The traditional rendering “asleep in Jesus” follows the second reading. The Greek word order allows either.

verse.text: For this we tell you by a word of the Lord: we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will certainly not go ahead of those who have fallen asleep.

note.term: by a word of the Lord
note.traditional: by the word of the Lord

verse.note: Paul claims the Lord’s authority for what follows. This may refer to a saying of Jesus handed down in the tradition (whether or not it is recorded in the Gospels) or to a revelation given through a Christian prophet, possibly Paul himself. The Greek does not settle the question.

The Greek word means “arrival” or “presence,” and was the regular term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city. A first-century reader would likely have heard that royal overtone in “the coming of the Lord.”

verse.text: For the Lord himself, with a shout of command, with an archangel’s voice and with God’s trumpet, will come down from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first;
then we who are alive, who are left, will be snatched up together with them in clouds to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will always be with the Lord.
verse.note: The verb means to seize or carry off suddenly and forcefully; “snatched” conveys this more directly than the traditional “caught up.” The Latin translation of this word is the source of the later term “rapture.”

The Greek noun was often used for the custom of a city’s residents going out to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him in. Many scholars think Paul’s picture draws on that custom, with believers going out to meet the arriving Lord; others doubt that the word carries this technical sense here. The text itself says only that from then on they will always be with the Lord.

verse.text: So then, encourage one another with these words.
Now about the times and the seasons, brothers and sisters, you have no need for anything to be written to you,
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine, but it was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members of a community. Since the letter is addressed to the whole assembly, “brothers and sisters” conveys what the first hearers understood. Several modern translations do the same; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

verse.text: for you yourselves know very well that the day of the Lord comes just like a thief in the night.
verse.note: The phrase comes from Israel’s prophets, where it names the day when God intervenes to judge and to rescue. Paul applies it to the coming of the Lord Jesus described at the end of the previous chapter.

verse.text: When people are saying, “Peace and security,” then sudden destruction comes upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will certainly not escape.
verse.note: Many scholars hear in this an echo of Roman imperial propaganda, which advertised peace and security as the benefits of Roman rule. Others think Paul is echoing the prophets’ charge against those who cry “Peace” when there is no peace. The two are not exclusive, and the allusion is not certain.

verse.text: But you, brothers and sisters, are not in darkness, so that the day should overtake you like a thief,
for you are all children of light and children of the day. We do not belong to the night or to darkness.
So then, let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us stay awake and be sober.
For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who get drunk are drunk at night.
But since we belong to the day, let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and as a helmet the hope of salvation.
For God did not appoint us for wrath but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ,
who died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with him.

note.term: whether we are awake or asleep

verse.note: The verbs are the same ones used in verse 6 for moral alertness and moral slumber. Most interpreters take them here to mean being alive or dead when the Lord comes, picking up the concern of 4:13–18. A minority reads them as still meaning watchful or unwatchful.

verse.text: Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as you are in fact doing.
Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, to recognize those who labor among you and lead you in the Lord and admonish you,
verse.note: The Greek verb can mean to preside over or lead, and also to care for or give aid to. Both senses were current, and translations divide between “are over you” or “have charge of you” and “care for you.” The three descriptions in this verse share one article in Greek and describe a single group of people.

verse.text: and to esteem them most highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
And we urge you, brothers and sisters: admonish the disorderly, comfort the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone.

note.traditional: the idle (many modern versions); the unruly (KJV)

verse.note: The word describes someone out of line or undisciplined, originally of soldiers who break rank. Many modern versions have “idle” because the related words in 2 Thessalonians 3:6–11 are used of people who refuse to work, and papyri use them of shirking duties. The word itself is broader than laziness, so “disorderly” is used here.

verse.text: See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good, both for one another and for everyone.
Rejoice always,
pray without ceasing,
give thanks in everything; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.
Do not quench the Spirit,
do not treat prophecies with contempt,
but test everything; keep hold of what is good,
keep away from every kind of evil.

note.traditional: all appearance of evil (KJV); every form of evil

verse.note: The Greek noun can mean outward appearance or kind, sort. The KJV’s “appearance of evil” has been widely taken to mean avoiding whatever merely looks wrong, but most scholars and modern versions take the sense here to be “every kind” or “every form” of evil. The verb echoes the one in verse 21, a play the translation keeps with “keep hold of” and “keep away from.”

verse.text: Now may the God of peace himself make you holy through and through, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek verb is built directly on the ordinary word for “holy,” and “make holy” keeps that link visible. Most traditional versions have “sanctify,” which means the same thing but now suggests a technical doctrine to many readers. The meaning is not disputed; the choice is one of clarity.

Some have read this as a formal statement that a human being has three parts. Most scholars take it as a piling up of terms for the whole person, in keeping with the stress on “through and through” and “whole” in the same sentence.
The Greek word means arrival or presence, and it was commonly used for the official visit of a ruler or high dignitary to a city. Paul uses it for the arrival of Jesus as Lord.

verse.text: The one who calls you is faithful, and he will do it.
Brothers and sisters, pray for us.
Greet all the brothers and sisters with a holy kiss.
I put you under oath by the Lord that this letter be read to all the brothers and sisters.

note.term: I put you under oath by the Lord
note.traditional: I charge you by the Lord

verse.note: The verb is strong: it binds the recipients by oath, with the Lord as the one sworn by. The letter shifts here from “we” to “I,” probably Paul speaking for himself. Letters were read aloud to the gathered community, and Paul insists that no one be left out.

verse.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
